"Across history, a persistent and seductive belief holds that 'great men'—exceptionally talented, courageous, or charismatic individuals—shape and redirect the course of events by virtue of their genius and personality. This 19th-century idea, championed by figures like Thomas Carlyle, presents leaders such as Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Martin Luther and Muhammad as singular catalysts of universal history, with the masses relegated to the passive roles of spectators, admirers and followers. Despite the rise of egalitarian and Marxist theories and later movements such as EP Thompson’s 'history from below', which emphasise popular forces, structural factors and collective action, the cult of exceptional individuals endures. It continues to animate those—disproportionately men—who see themselves cast in a heroic mould, convinced they possess a unique mission, insight, or sacred duty to lead, save, or transform nations. These self-appointed saviours are often ruthless and arrogant enough to impose their will on others. Crucially, the text argues that in the modern context these proclaimed 'great' men frequently fail to be genuine heroes; rather, they resemble anti-heroes or outright villains. Though they command significant power, their exercise of it tends to be damaging rather than ennobling. In short, the romanticised image of solitary, superior individuals steering history is both an anachronistic conceit and a dangerous one, because it masks how authority can be abused and how genuine historical change more often involves broader social forces than solitary genius."
